questions.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curves $(x+y)^{3}-y=0$ and $(x+y)^{2}-y=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{3}-y=0\,⟹\,{u}^{3}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x+y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{2}-y=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{3} \\ v={u}^{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}(u-1)=0 \\ v=u.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation 

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,{u}^{3}\le v\le {u}^{2}\}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186104/assets/a8d2549c665a918cc8d69c69136fcb49e654ebb9aa5e53611155798e791b36a9.png)

   

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|1|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{u}^{3}}^{{u}^{2}}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}v{|}_{{u}^{3}}^{{u}^{2}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}-{u}^{3})du \\  & ={[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{u}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=y+3x,\,v=x,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(y+3x)^{2}-x=3$ and the line $x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=y+3x,\,v=x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $y+3x=u$ and $x=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3x)^{2}-x=3\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=3\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}-3,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x=1\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2}-3 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 2 \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,{u}^{2}-3\le v\le 1\}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186104/assets/2687f0cc14eb0b476ea5f4ba7272e7f248bb7dcb276a0e2b0c39e551501b011d.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(-1)^{-1}=-1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-1|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}-3}^{1}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[v]_{{u}^{2}-3}^{1}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(1-({u}^{2}-3))\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & ={[4u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =16-\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the following curves and lines.

$$
y=\frac{5}{{e}^{x}},\,y=\frac{12}{{e}^{x}},\,2y-1=0,\,2y-5=0
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv,
$$

  

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
{e}^{x}y=5,\,{e}^{x}y=12,\,2y=1,\,2y=5
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u={e}^{x}y,\,v=2y
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u={e}^{x}y$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x}y=5\,\text{ }\,⟹\,u=5 \\  & {e}^{x}y=12\,⟹\,u=12\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=2y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 2y=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & 2y=5\,⟹\,v=5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,5\le u\le 12,\,1\le v\le 5\}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186104/assets/615d6822e60e9b5ff646497e14df1468e1fd09ee67fab5c334b635d130f16f14.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}y & {e}^{x} \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2{e}^{x}y \\  & =2u.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{2u}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{5}^{12}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{5}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(12)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5))\cdot (5-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{12}{5})\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the following lines.

$$
3y=4x+1,\,3y=4x-2,\,3x=2y+1,\,3x=2y+3
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv,
$$

  

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
4x-3y=-1,\,4x-3y=2,\,3x-2y=1,\,3x-2y=3
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u=4x-3y,\,v=3x-2y
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=4x-3y$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 4x-3y=-1\,⟹\,u=-1 \\  & 4x-3y=2\,⟹\,u=2\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=3x-2y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 3x-2y=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & 3x-2y=3\,⟹\,v=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186104/assets/5dc4be989300dca3e52b7ff1dfb6a21c60409976fe55d42f5ae530f033725a64.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-8+9 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}v \\  & =(2-(-1))\cdot (3-1) \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{1}{xy},\,v={x}^{2}y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
y=\frac{1}{2x},\,y=\frac{1}{3x},\,y=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,y=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=\frac{1}{xy},\,v={x}^{2}y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=\frac{1}{xy}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{2x} & ⟹\, & \frac{1}{xy}=2 & ⟹\, & u=2 \\  & y=\frac{1}{3x} & ⟹\, & \frac{1}{xy}=3 & ⟹\, & u=3\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v={x}^{2}y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹\, & {x}^{2}y=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹\, & {x}^{2}y=3 & ⟹\, & v=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186104/assets/05d2ca47db245b147cb52f95a474a60ece144931c8b6e1e40c6628a99b53d690.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y} & -\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}} \\ 2xy & \text{ }\text{ }{x}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=y=\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}=\frac{1}{{u}^{2}v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}v}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =(-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2})\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$
